span.span: To accurately identify a patient’s Fitzpatrick skin tone group from an image, follow these detailed steps:

1. Understand the Fitzpatrick Skin Tone Classification: - Type I: Always burns, never tans (pale white; blond or red hair; blue eyes; freckles). This type has very light skin that is highly sensitive to the sun. - Type II: Usually burns, tans minimally (white; fair; red or blond hair; blue, hazel, or green eyes). This type has light skin that burns easily but can tan slightly. - Type III: Sometimes mild burn, tans uniformly (cream white; fair with golden undertone; dark blonde hair; blue, green, or brown eyes). This type has a light to medium skin tone that tans well but can still burn. - Type IV: Burns minimally, always tans well (beige; typical Mediterranean skin tone; brown hair; brown eyes). This type has a medium skin tone that tans easily and rarely burns. - Type V: Very rarely burns, tans very easily (brown; typical Middle Eastern skin tones; dark brown hair; brown eyes). This type has a darker skin tone that tans very easily and almost never burns. - Type VI: Never burns, tans very deeply (black; very dark brown; black hair; dark brown eyes). This type has the darkest skin tone that never burns and tans very deeply.

2. Analyze the Image: - Color and Undertones: Observe the overall color of the skin. Determine if it is very light, light, medium, dark, or very dark. Note any undertones such as golden, beige, reddish, etc. For example, a light skin with a golden undertone might suggest Type III. - Freckles and Moles: Note the presence of freckles, moles, or any other pigmentation. Freckles are more common in lighter skin types (Types I and II). Moles can be present in all skin types but are more noticeable in lighter skin. - Signs of Sun Damage: Look for signs of aging, discoloration, or other sun-related damage. Sun damage is more visible in lighter skin types. For example, if there are signs of sun damage on a light skin, it might suggest Type I or II. - Hair and Eye Color: Note the hair and eye color as they can provide additional clues. For example, dark hair and eyes are more common in darker skin types (Types V and VI). Light hair and eyes are more common in lighter skin types (Types I and II).

3. Match the Image to the Fitzpatrick Scale: Use the observations from step 2 to match the skin in the image to the closest Fitzpatrick skin type. Consider the skin’s natural color, its reaction to the sun, and any other relevant features. Pay attention to the undertones and the presence of freckles or sun damage. For example, if the skin is light with freckles and signs of sun damage, it is likely to be Type I or II.

4. Select the Correct Choice: The choices provided will be in the format ’XY’, where ’X’ and ’Y’ represent two consecutive Fitzpatrick skin types. For example, ’12’ represents types I and II, ’34’ represents types III and IV, and ’56’ represents types V and VI. Based on your analysis, select the choice that best matches the skin type you have identified. If the skin appears to be a medium to dark brown color with a significant amount of melanin and no visible signs of freckles or light complexion, it is more likely to be types V or VI.

5. Requirements: - Always use the provided list of skin tone groups. - Ensure your reasoning is based on the Fitzpatrick skin tone classification. - Provide a clear and concise explanation for your choice. - Consider the undertones, presence of freckles, and hair and eye color when making your decision.
